candidate_analysis.explanation: The Random Forest predicts MALWARE with probability 1.0000, and all 20 top n-grams push toward cryptojacking (SHAP +0.0062 to +0.0143). No n-gram pushes the other way. Several of the n-grams fit the instruction mix of hashing and mining kernels. MOVDQA PAND (rank 2, +0.012515, freq 0.008550), PAND PXOR (rank 16, +0.007721) and PXOR PXOR (rank 15, +0.007742) show SIMD bitwise masking and XOR mixing. MOV ROL (rank 8, +0.008778) and ROL ADD (rank 10, +0.008327) show rotate-and-add sequences, as in ARX-style or hash-round arithmetic. SHRD BT (rank 4, +0.010097) and MOV SHRD (rank 12, +0.008065) suggest multi-word shifts and bit testing, as in wide-integer or bit-manipulation code. The floating-point and conversion patterns (MOV FLD, ADD FLD, CVTTSD2SI LEA) and the conditional-move pattern (SUB CMOVG) add smaller contributions, and their link to mining is less direct. The remaining top features (MOV RET, PUSH RET, CALL PUSH, POP PUSH, POP SUB, POP XOR, POP CALL, LEA JC, MOV MOVZX) are generic control-flow and stack idioms. They carry high SHAP weight, but on their own they are not specific to cryptojacking. The evidence lists no function names or API references, so I cannot tie any pattern to a particular routine. My high-confidence call rests on the model's certainty and the consistent direction of all 20 SHAP values, plus the cluster of rotate/XOR/SIMD-logic n-grams. It is not a confirmed identification of a mining algorithm.

evidence_analysis.assessment: Generic function-epilogue idiom. It is the strongest single contributor, but it likely reflects the binary's overall code structure rather than a mining-specific behavior.
Aligned 128-bit SIMD load followed by a bitwise AND. At 0.85% frequency it is a fairly prominent pattern. It is consistent with vectorized masking in hashing or cipher-like compute loops.

Byte-extraction and zero-extension pattern. It is common in table-lookup and byte-wise data processing, and at 2.7% frequency it is the most frequent n-gram listed. Mildly consistent with hash or cipher state handling but not specific.
Double-precision shift followed by a bit test. This is an unusual pairing that suggests wide-integer arithmetic or bit-level manipulation, and it may reflect compute-heavy numeric code.
Stack restore followed by a subtraction. This is a generic idiom, and its weight probably reflects model-learned structure rather than a direct mining indicator.
Unusual control-flow idiom (push then return). It may point to non-standard control flow or compiler/packer artifacts, but the evidence does not say which.
Call followed by a stack push. This is a generic call-sequence pattern with limited standalone diagnostic value.
Load or move followed by a bitwise rotate. Rotates are a core primitive in many hash and cipher rounds, so this supports a mining-kernel interpretation.
Register save/restore shuffling. Generic, and likely a prologue/epilogue artifact.
Rotate followed by an add is characteristic of ARX-style mixing in hash rounds. Together with MOV ROL it is one of the more algorithm-relevant signals.
Stack pop followed by an XOR. It may be register zeroing or mixing after a restore. Weakly informative alone.
Move feeding a double-precision shift. Reinforces the SHRD BT signal for wide-integer or bit-level manipulation.
Load into the x87 floating-point stack. This indicates floating-point computation. Its link to mining is not direct, and it may reflect numeric helper code.
Subtract followed by a conditional move. This is branchless min/max or clamping logic that is common in tight compute loops. At 0.11% frequency it is moderately informative.
Consecutive SIMD XORs. This suggests vectorized state mixing or register clearing, which fits hashing and cipher kernels.
SIMD AND followed by XOR. Together with MOVDQA PAND and PXOR PXOR it forms a cluster of SIMD bitwise-logic patterns typical of hash computation.
Stack restore followed by a call. A generic control-flow pattern with low specificity.
Address computation followed by a jump on carry. This suggests carry-dependent logic, possibly multi-precision arithmetic, but the evidence is thin because the frequency is very low.
Add followed by an x87 floating-point load. It indicates mixed integer and floating-point processing and has a weak, indirect link to mining.

Double-to-integer truncating conversion followed by address calculation. This suggests floating-point values being used as indices or counts. It is weakly informative and could belong to many numeric workloads.
